title: An Interesting, Vastly Incomplete Look at Baseball Cards
summary: Josh and Chuck open with news of their Podcast Academy Governor's Award and their hesitations about baseball card terminology, then trace the history of baseball cards: 1869 Peck and Snyder Cincinnati Red Stockings card, 1880s tobacco cards from Duke and Old Judge (N167), the Tobacco-era T206 set and the Honus Wagner card, the golden age of candy and gum-packaged cards, Bowman and Topps' near-monopoly and the Haelan v. Topps case on likeness rights, Topps' 1957 card size and the dumping of unsold 1952-era cards, the 1980s rise of the adult collecting market and conventions, modern inserts and memorabilia cards, gambling-like pack buying, counterfeiting and authentication (PSA), and the Billy Ripken "F face" card. The episode closes with a listener mail correction about the Amber Room and Catherine the Great, and a correction about the term "proxy war."

segments.title: Opening banter and Governor's Award
segments.summary: Hosts discuss receiving the Podcast Academy's Governor's Award in Las Vegas and their admitted limited expertise on baseball cards, and Chuck's and Josh's personal collecting histories.

segments.title: Earliest trade cards and the 1869 Peck and Snyder card
segments.summary: Early trade cards were business cards with baseball images; the 1869 Cincinnati Red Stockings card by Peck and Snyder is usually called the first baseball card, though the Library of Congress counts a souvenir team photo.

segments.title: Tobacco cards and the N162/N167 Old Judge sets
segments.summary: Tobacco companies, including Duke, put cardboard cards in cigarette packs starting in the 1880s; Old Judge included baseball players in 1886 and released the N167 set, considered the first official set. Cards were random premiums and early cards faded and were glued photographs.

segments.title: Non-standard early era and candy/gum cards
segments.summary: Early baseball cards appeared in many random places, such as magazines and biscuit boxes. Around the early 1900s, cards moved into caramel and candy packaging, including round and die-cut shapes, to avoid selling cigarettes to children.

segments.title: T206 set and the Honus Wagner card
segments.summary: The T206 tobacco set (about 1909 to 1911) is famous mainly because of the Honus Wagner card, which was scarce partly because Wagner objected to his likeness selling cigarettes, and partly because a 1937 price guide overstated its rarity. It sold for about $7.25 million in recent years, while other T206 cards cost much less.

segments.title: Bowman, Topps monopoly, and Haelan v. Topps likeness case
segments.summary: After World War II, Bowman and then Topps professionalized baseball cards. Topps obtained exclusive contracts with players and held a near-monopoly from the early 1950s to about 1980, ending when players stopped signing. Haelan Laboratories sued Topps in 1953, leading to a legal recognition of publicity rights over one's likeness.

segments.title: Sy Berger, standard card size, and the 1952 Topps dump
segments.summary: Topps' Sy Berger standardized card design, including the 1957 3.5 by 2.5 inch size, team logos, color, and stats on the back. Unsold 1952 Topps cards were dumped in the ocean around 1960, which made surviving 1952 cards rare, including a Mickey Mantle that sold for about $12.6 million.

segments.title: Modern collecting boom, conventions, and overproduction
segments.summary: Adult collecting grew from the first West Coast convention in 1969 to the first National Sports Collectors Convention in 1980s. Demand from baby boomers in the 1970s and 1980s was followed by overproduction in the 1990s, when Upper Deck introduced higher-quality cards and extras, leading to the junk wax era.

segments.title: Modern inserts, memorabilia cards, gambling concerns, and counterfeits
segments.summary: Modern cards embed memorabilia like bat pieces and hair, and pack-based chase for valuable cards has drawn RICO and gambling-style lawsuits, including one against Panini that is still ongoing. Counterfeits have grown more convincing, and authenticators like Professional Sports Authenticator (PSA) verify cards, with a counterfeit slab detected by a missing period. Rookie cards are valued largely by tradition. The Billy Ripken 1989 Fleer 'F face' error card is a notable exception to error cards being valuable.

segments.title: Listener mail: Amber Room and Catherine the Great
segments.summary: Listener Rebecca corrects the earlier Amber Room episode, explaining the Russian succession from Peter the Great through Elizabeth to Catherine the Great, and describes visiting the Catherine Palace.

segments.title: Proxy war correction and sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts correct an earlier misuse of the term 'proxy war' regarding NATO and Russia in Ukraine in the Louisiana Purchase episode, then sign off with contact information.
